title: Does a stock humanoid pay for itself on a house site, and how much of a new home's price could it remove?
summary: Prices the 46 crew-hours of buildbot-taskbook against the ownership cost of a Unitree G1 ($16,000 launch price) or H1 ($90,000) and a $29.12/h carpenter median (BLS, May 2025). A robot may take only the tasks whose static payload test it passes (H1 32.7 h, G1 5.9 h). The net saving per replaced crew-hour is the loaded wage less slowdown × (ownership rate + supervision × wage), so there is a break-even slowdown: about 2.4 robot-hours per crew-hour for the G1 and 1.1 for the H1 at 0.3 supervision. Over a 4,000-draw sweep the G1 saves money in 15% of draws and the H1 in 0.4%; the best draw saves about $200 on this scope, and a free instant H1 would remove $1,217, 0.18% of NAHB's $665,298 average price. A crude cost-scaled scenario (hours matched to NAHB's framing share) gives up to 8.1% as a ceiling. Slowdown, supervision, success, burden, life and upkeep are swept, not measured: no robot skill is simulated yet, prices are 2024 launch figures, and payload passes are upper bounds.
lede: does a stock humanoid pay for itself on a house site? The break-even slowdown against a $38/h loaded carpenter is about 2.4 for a $16k Unitree G1 and 1.1 for a $90k H1; over a sweep the G1 saves money in 15% of draws, the H1 in 0.4%, and a perfect H1 would remove 0.19% of an average home's price on the taskbook scope (inputs swept, not measured).
